Yes—there are a few useful things you can do while you wait:

1) Make sure the toilet can’t refill/overflow again  
- If you haven’t already, turn the shutoff valve behind the toilet fully clockwise.  
- If there’s no accessible valve, leave the tank lid off and make sure no one flushes that toilet.

2) Remove as much dirty water as possible  
- Prioritize getting water away from:
  - Doorways and hallways
  - Wood/laminate floors
  - Any carpet or rugs  
- Use towels to move water toward the tub/shower drain area if it’s easier, then wring them out there.

3) Disinfect the floor (important: it’s toilet water)  
Once most standing water is gone:  
- Mix a disinfectant solution (for example: household bleach diluted in water per label, or any bathroom disinfectant cleaner).  
- Wipe/mop the entire wet area, especially around the toilet base and where the water spread.  
- After disinfecting, go over once more with clean water if the cleaner recommends it.

4) Start drying to prevent mold/warping  
- Open the bathroom door and any nearby windows.  
- If you have a fan, aim it into the bathroom across the floor.  
- If towels get soaked, swap them for dry ones so they keep pulling moisture out.

5) Check nearby areas  
- If there’s a room below the bathroom, quickly check its ceiling for any wet spots or drips.  
- If you see new dripping or bulging paint, note the location so you can tell the plumber—don’t poke it, just keep a bucket under it if it drips.

6) Watch for any new plumbing symptoms  
- If you notice:
  - Other toilets gurgling,
  - Water coming up in the tub/shower or sink drains,
  - Drains suddenly getting very slow,
  stop using water as much as possible and tell the plumber this when they respond.
